analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to 56 hours, about seven days, of paid sick leave a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote; it sat in three House committees until the Congress ended in January 2023, despite 162 House cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year. The time could be used for a worker's own illness or medical care, to care for a sick child or family member, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Businesses with fewer than 15 employees could choose to provide the same time unpaid instead. Workers could enforce the right in court and the Labor Department would investigate complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without paid sick time, especially low-wage workers: the bill's own findings say 55 percent of the lowest-earning private-sector workers lack paid sick time, along with more than 80 percent of food preparation and serving workers. Workers also gain the right to paid time off for a sick child or family member, not just themselves, and protected leave for dealing with domestic violence or stalking. Public health also benefits on paper: the findings cite a study finding flu rates fell 5.5 to 6.5 percent in cities that adopted paid sick time laws.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for the worker's own illness, medical appointments, family care, or situations arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

It is unlawful for an employer to interfere with, deny, or retaliate against a worker for using or asking for sick time, and workers can sue in federal or state court with attorney's fees, while the Labor Department investigates complaints.
Employers with an existing paid leave policy at least as generous are exempt, and stronger state or local sick leave laws are not overridden, so the bill sets a floor rather than a ceiling.

The bill's findings cite studies estimating a universal paid sick days policy would cut preventable emergency room visits and save about $1.1 billion a year, including $500 million for Medicare and Medicaid, and would reduce the spread of flu-like illness.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would pay up to 56 hours of wages per employee per year when the time is used, plus recordkeeping and compliance costs. The heaviest relative burden falls on industries that employ the most workers without paid sick time today, such as food service, retail, and hospitality. Smaller employers can shift the cost to workers by offering the 56 hours unpaid.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially in low-wage service industries

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a genuine wage cost for employers of up to seven paid days per employee per year, falling hardest on low-margin businesses that already employ the most workers without sick leave; the bill text and findings contain no independent estimate of employer-side costs.

Employers with fewer than 15 workers may opt out of paying for the leave and instead provide 56 hours unpaid, which means some of the lowest-paid workers, the ones least able to lose a day's pay, could still face the choice between unpaid time off and going to work sick.

Employers may require a doctor's certification for sick time covering more than three consecutive workdays, and no paid time can be used until the 60th day of employment, both of which add friction for workers in hourly jobs where getting to a doctor is difficult.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is direct and concrete: paid time to see a doctor, recover, or care for a sick child without losing wages or a job, with court enforcement behind it. The cost is real but modest in design terms: the accrual rate caps the mandate at about seven days a year, exempts employers with equally generous existing policies, and lets very small firms substitute unpaid leave. The main honest criticism is the small-employer opt-out, which leaves the lowest-wage workers partially uncovered, and the absence of an independent estimate of what the mandate costs employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended, so it died automatically.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on April 13, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Education and Labor, House Administration, and Oversight and Reform.
162 House members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.

The bill's only recorded actions are its introduction and the three committee referrals; no committee reported it, no vote was ever held in either chamber, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill.
This was a long-running proposal: identical Healthy Families Act bills had been introduced in prior Congresses without becoming law, and the Senate never took up a companion version in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly those in food service, retail, and other low-wage industries that employ the most workers without paid sick time, are better off because the mandate never took effect and they avoided paying up to 56 hours of leave per employee. Workers who lack paid sick time, whom the bill's findings put at 29 percent of the private-sector workforce, remain without it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided the paid-leave mandate

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act and recruited 162 cosponsors.

for.name: 162 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote in two years despite the Democratic majority and 162 cosponsors.

against.name: Chair Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in the committee with primary jurisdiction; the committee reported no action.

against.name: Business groups opposing paid sick leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Long opposed federal paid sick leave mandates as a cost and compliance burden on employers; no member of Congress moved to advance the bill in committee or on the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 162 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; because it never reached a vote, there is no roll-call breakdown, but the sponsorship pattern was entirely one-sided.

industries.note: These industries would bear the mandate's wage cost, and they employ the workers most likely to lack paid sick time today, so their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the workers' interest in getting it.

They could opt out of paying for leave entirely and substitute 56 hours of unpaid time, a much lighter burden than larger employers face, though recordkeeping and notice requirements would still apply.

Public agencies are covered employers and states accepting federal financial assistance would waive immunity to employee suits, so governments would face the same paid-leave mandate and litigation exposure as private employers.
